column2: the writer's notes (doubts; where the article disagrees with the entry): for the data check

The article dates the Girón Agreement both to 27 February and to 28 February 1829 (La Mar's signature); the text says only that it was signed after the battle. The entry says the victory saved Guayaquil; the article says Guayaquil stayed in Peruvian hands until it was returned on 20 July 1829 under the Piura Armistice. The text gives the dates without judging which act saved it. Troop numbers: the article estimates 5,000 Gran Colombian against 4,500 Peruvian troops, while Sucre's inscription claimed 4,000 against 8,000; both are given, the second as the inscription's claim.

The article's sources are Herodotus and Pausanias only; it gives no date for the battle itself, only the 550-546 BCE frame for the later recovery of the bones. The entry's c. 560 BCE is not contradicted and is not repeated. Short article (about 500 words, much of it a quotation); the text keeps close to it.

The article names Viguera and Castile as Galib's allies; the entry says Castile and Pamplona. The text names only the two leaders the article gives and does not mention Pamplona. The entry places the site in the province of Soria; the article says only near Atienza. The province is not repeated. The article says the campaign lasted seventy-eight days and ended in Córdoba on 27 July; from 11 May that is closer to 77 days. Neither figure is printed. The article also notes the Anales castellanos segundos record the taking of Atienza under the Spanish era year corresponding to 980, though the year was 981; left out.

Tony Jaques (2007) dated the battle to 431, against the entry's 440s; that date is left out. De Boone (1954) argued for the winter of 442-3, rejected by Lanting and van der Plicht; left out as outside the entry's 440s frame only in part and as superseded. The entry says Chlodio kept the lands up to the Somme; the article says only that the Franks expanded towards the Somme. Not contradicted.
The article dates the Santiago del Estero deputies' Congress to 20 March 1820 and Ibarra's victory to 31 March 1820, though the republic's constitution came only in September; left out.

The article says Berthold died probably in 1088; the entry's d. 1088 is kept and not hedged further. The article does not mention the first record of the counts of Zollern in 1061 that the entry names.

The article's lead describes the complex as founded by Bhoja in the 11th century, while its own later text says the building mainly dates to the 12th-13th centuries and that the name Bhojshala dates from 1903. The text gives both as the article attributes them. The article (in a partisan-sounding passage) compares the complex to Nalanda and Taxila; left out as an unsourced claim. The 2026 ruling is told as a dated fact with the objection of Jain experts; no verdict on the dispute.
Liam Kelley's argument appeared on a personal blog according to the article; the text names him as a historian and does not mention the blog.

The entry mentions labour provided for Egyptian estates, which the article does not mention; left out. The article spells the name Biridiya, Biridya and Biridija, and Labaya also as Labayu; the text keeps Labaya, with Labayu only in the letter's title.

The entry names the fine imposed by King Thibaw's court in 1885 and calls the company the largest extractor of teak in Burma; the article says only that it was a leading producer of teak and that its conflict with the Burmese state served as a pretext. The text keeps to the article's wording and does not repeat the fine. The article says the Rangoon business shipped tea to Bombay and was set up for the Burmese tea business; this is probably a slip for teak, so the commodity of the Rangoon business is left unnamed.
The article's Status section uses loaded wording (infiltrators who stole status); the text states the counts and the effect on Manchu soldiers' posts without that wording.

One tradition says he reached Gazargamu and studied there after his release; another says he went home. The text says only that he set out for it. The entry says he helped open the way for the founding of Muri; the article says his lieutenant Hamma Ruwa conquered it by 1817 and that Bello later made it independent of Gombe. Not contradicted.

The article dates the manuscript's arrival at the Bodleian to 1627 or 1629; the entry gives 1627. The year is left out. The article gives 1,641 lines for the incomplete manuscript; the entry's about 1,600 is not repeated.

The entry says the Caeté were enslaved or destroyed after 1556; the article also tells of a migration north in the 1580s, a Captaincy of Caeté (1622-1753) and about 135 descendants today. The text tells the northern migration as Caeté groups moving north and does not give the descendants' number. The entry places their lands between Pernambuco and the São Francisco; the article from the São Francisco's mouth to Itamaracá. Not contradictory. The article's population estimate of 300-2,000 people in the early 1500s seems inconsistent with the scale of the wars; left out.
Short article (about 360 words); the text may fall near the lower word limit. David Bowles, a translator who agrees with Garibay and León-Portilla, is not named.

The article gives about 1,100 men sent to New France; the entry says roughly 1,200. Neither figure is printed. The article says roughly 400 and, later, about 450 stayed as settlers; the entry says more than 400. No figure is printed. Captain de Monteil's journal claimed 400 men died of cold on the first expedition, against the Jesuit Relations' over 60; only the latter is given.

SKIPPED: Article of about 340 words, most of it already in the entry; what remains (the name's medieval origin, the headland's height and shape, the arable land) is too little for 260 words. The article's lead says both that the site dates from the 3rd century BC and that it was built in the first half of the 4th century BC; the entry gives the 4th-2nd centuries BCE.

The entry says the princes ruled under the Western Turks before the 8th-century conquests; the article says the territories north of the Oxus fell under Western Turk suzerainty after 567 and that Chaghan Khudah rule is attested by the late 7th century. Not contradicted. Sources differ on Abu 'Ali's successor (a grandson Abu'l Muzaffar ibn Muhammad, or Abu'l-Hasan Taher); left out.
The article's claim that Nasser started and funded the 1956 uprising is reported only as 'is said to'; the text attributes it to some.
The article gives his death both as 10 June and as 14 June 1824; the text gives no day. The entry dates his base at Paspébiac from 1766; the article gives no year for it. Not repeated.
The article also describes a second French fort built by Strozzi's men in 1577-1578 (130 feet a side); only summarised here.
SKIPPED: article under 250 words of substance; the entry already gives its contents, the four sections apart

The article says the chronicle covers 76 kings until 1955; the entry says it continues into the 19th century. Neither end date is printed. The article dates the oldest extant copy to the early 19th century under Ching-Thang Khomba (Bhagyachandra), but elsewhere places his redrafting in the mid- to late 18th century; the copy's date is left out.
The article spells the temple both Tiruvanchaikkalam (in the legend) and Thiruvanchikulam (in Kodungallur); both kept as given.

The article lists El Salvador, Venezuela, Nicaragua, Honduras and Panama as adopting it as well as Ecuador and Colombia; the entry names only the latter two as adopting it almost unchanged, which this does not contradict.

The article tells Wellesley's treaty twice, once dated 1806 and once 1809, and mixes the Treaty of Lahore (1806) with the 1809 treaty; only the 1809 treaty's date and terms are used. The article does not name the 1809 treaty as the Treaty of Amritsar, as the entry does; it is called the treaty of 25 April 1809 here.

The article dates the building of the mounds and pyramids (phase Cochasquí II) to about 1250-1550, and its lead says the site was built by the Caranqui between 1250 and 1550; the entry says it was built from around 950 until the Inca conquest. The 1250 date is left out; the text says only that the first settlers of around 950 built no mounds. The article spells the park 'Arcaheological'; corrected in the text.
The article gives her birth as c. 1640 and her death as c. 1686 in the lead but 1686 later; the entry has d. 1686.

The article's lead gives the committee's span as 15 August to 7 September 1945, but its body says it was dissolved into the People's Republic Executive Committee on 7 October; no dissolution date is printed. The entry says its local committees took over administration across Korea; the article does not describe this.

The article describes the group as gathering around the Pott brothers in the late autumn of 1714, with Gruber and Rock among the early leaders; the entry names Gruber and Rock as the founders. The text does not say who founded it. The article dates the emigration only to the 1840s; the entry's 1843 is not contradicted.
The article's title name is the African Company of Merchants; the entry's name is used.

The article gives the sessions as 6 May to 14 October 1821, consistent with the entry; the specific days are not printed. The article's wording on Cúcuta as the 'birthplace of Bolívar's dream' of a single federal state is left out as rhetoric; the republic was centralised.

The entry says the army won the civil war of 1915; the article says the main fighting was over by 1917 and that the war was won only after Zapata's assassination in 1919 and Villa's surrender in July 1920. No date for the victory is printed. The entry names Villa among its commanders; the article says Villa gave only theoretical support before turning against Carranza. The text says only that support was given in theory.
The article says nothing of the Mississippian towns, the Little Egypt site or Coosa that the entry names. The article's dates for New Echota '(1794-1907)' are garbled; not used.

The entry says they were later subject to the Eóganacht kings of Iarmumu; the article says they were under the nominal overlordship of the Eóganacht Locha Léin in Iarmuman for at least some time, and likely had an independent existence in the first millennium. The text keeps to 'at least some time'.
The article calls the party the National Front (NF); the entry calls it the National Liberation Front. The article's name is used.
SKIPPED: article under 250 words, mostly repeating the entry; it also dates the abolition to 1935 against the entry's 1937

The entry says the county was centred on Tremp; the article gives its capital as Segur and says it had a frontier with the Moorish Conca de Tremp, while also naming Pobla de Segur and Tremp as the economic centre of Pallars by 1000. Tremp and the capital were left out. The entry says the county passed to the counts of Barcelona in 1192; the article says Dolça de Só donated it to Alfonso and the Crown of Aragon (specifically the Kingdom of Aragon). Worded as the article has it, without contradicting the entry.

The article says the Covenant Chain continued until 1753, when the Mohawk declared it broken, but also that Johnson renewed it in 1755; the entry says it underpinned cooperation until the American Revolution. The phrase 'continued until 1753' was left out; the 1753 declaration and the 1755 renewal are told. The article's long quotation from Howard Zinn was not used.

The article gives Ahaya's death as 1783 in its lead but says 'After Ahaya's death in 1784' later; the entry has d. 1783. The text says only that he died soon after the 1783 cession. Some sources make Cowkeeper the same man as Secoffee; Kenneth Porter argues they were different people. Left out. Bartram's visit is dated 1773 in one place and 1774 in another; no year given.
SKIPPED: article has about 250 words, most of them already in the entry's description

The article gives the naturalisation of foreigners both as 'not earlier than the fourth generation' (lead) and 'after three generations in the north and possibly as many as nine elsewhere'; the text uses the latter, for the north only. The Statute of Rhuddlan (1284) superseding the criminal codes was left out to keep to the entry's 'partly in use until the Laws in Wales Acts'.

The article gives the hill as 534 metres (1,753 ft) high, which is likely its elevation above sea level rather than its height above the city; left out. The entry cites the Kano Chronicle; the article does not name it, so the text speaks of Kano tradition.

The entry calls Amari Ngoone Sobel Fall the first Damel; the article's list puts 'Dece Fu Njogu' in 1549 before Amary Ngone Sobel Fall (1549–1593). The text does not say who was first. The article says Alvise Cadamosto recorded the title Damel for the ruler of Cayor in the 1450s, a century before the entry's starting date of 1549; left out. The article's list ends with Meissa Tendi Dior Birima Demba War Sall, 1883–1902, which overlaps Samba Laobé Fall and runs past the entry's end date of 1886; left out.
The article's lead gives Malo's birth as 1795 (as the entry does), but its Life section says he was born around 1793. No birth year given in the text.

The entry says she retired to Mellifont Abbey, where she died; the article, citing the Annals of Ulster, Loch Cé and the Four Masters, says she retired to Clonmacnoise in 1186 and died there in 1193. The place of her retirement and death was left out. The Annals of the Four Masters record her return from Leinster in 1153 twice, once as taken back by force by Tairdelbach Ua Conchobair, once as her own choice; the text keeps to the neutral wording of the article's lead.

The article dates his reign c. 953–999 and notes that R. K. Dikshit (1976) placed its end in 1002, while S. K. Sullerey (2004) has 999; the entry has c. 950–999. No start or end year of the reign is given in the text.

The article names Sitawaka Rajasinghe as the king whose attacks forced the Portuguese out of Kotte in 1565; the entry names Mayadunne of Sitawaka as the rival who won over Dharmapala's subjects. Both are given as the article and the entry have them; no contradiction intended.

The article presents Dhian Singh's role in the deaths of Chet Singh, Kharak Singh, Nau Nihal Singh and Chand Kaur largely as fact, citing Gardner for Nau Nihal; the text keeps to what the article states and adds no further charge.

The article says he governed Nuevo León from 1588 to 1610 and died about 1611; the entry says he governed until his death. The end of his governorship was left out. The article dates the Chichimeca War episode with his third wife to 1550, which does not fit its own account of a first wife who came with him in 1548; the year was left out.

The entry names Đỗ Thích as the murderer; the article says the records are vague and inconsistent, that Đỗ Thích was executed without evidence and that the real assassin remains unconfirmed. The text neither names the assassin nor calls the question open. The article gives his birth as 945; the entry has '?'. No birth year given.

The entry says he succeeded Diwan Mohkam Chand in the financial administration; the article says he succeeded Diwan Ganga Ram in 1826 and Diwan Bhawani Das in 1834, and names Mokham Chand only in the acquisition of Kashmir. The text tells the article's successions without denying the entry's. The article gives the title Raja as conferred in 1847 (lead) and the title Raja Diwan as conferred in 1838 (Career); no year given for the title. Left out: the article's unsourced claim that under British rule he secretly financed independence efforts.

The article says he was taken to Lisbon aboard the ship Carrasco before his execution on Campo da Pólvora; the entry says he was executed in Salvador. The Lisbon voyage was left out, and the place is given as Campo da Pólvora only. His birthplace is disputed; the text gives the accepted version (Marataízes) and the alternatives the article names.

The article puts the Battle of Thurles in 1175 ('In 1175, having demolished the Cambro-Normans at the Battle of Thurles'); the entry has 1174. The text dates only the blinding to 1175 and gives no year for the battle.

SKIPPED: the article holds only geography, wildlife and a list of towns, with no history; a longer text would be padding. It also places the valley in Uttarakhand and Himachal Pradesh and calls Dehradun the winter capital, where the entry has Uttarakhand and the state capital

The article dates the submission at Dore to 827 in the Chronicle, 'more likely 829'; the entry gives 829, so the text says 827 is more likely 829. Left out: the claim that Egbert became 'the first king of all England at Dore' (the entry calls his northern overlordship brief), present-day councillors and MP's name, notable residents (mostly living people), Brinkburn Grange.

The article does not date the coins; the entry's '1st and 2nd centuries' is neither confirmed nor contradicted. The article says the site 'has not been subject to archaeological excavation' but also reports excavations in May 2025; the text says it was long unexcavated and gives the 2025 find. Purchase price (reportedly about EUR 1 million) left out.

The entry says Dubays was killed in 1135 on the orders of Sultan Mas'ud; the article says he was murdered by Assassins at the same time as al-Mustarshid, and that he remained closely tied to Mas'ud. The manner of his death is left out of the text. The article gives his death as 29 August 1135, consistent with the entry's year. The article does not say whether Zengi's offered exchange freed him; only the offer is told.

The article's lead says he commanded the French mission to the Hejaz 'from 1914 to 1916', but its body says he headed the mission from August 1916 to December 1917 and arrived at Alexandria on 1 September 1916; only the arrival dates are given. The Marash passage is paraphrased from his own words quoted in the article.
The article calls him 'sacked'; worded as recalled.

The article calls the battle site both Lugalo and Rugaro; the text names neither in the last section, the entry already naming Lugalo. Mkwawa's brother Mpangie and the farm-burning dates (5-6 and 15-16 August 1891) left out for length.

The article calls Cashel the capital of the 'early Catholic kingdom of Munster'; rendered as 'early Christian'. The article's list of kings ends with Donnchad (d. 963) but does not say he was the last; the text does not claim it.

The article reports a CFR honour conferred on him by President Buhari 'in October 2022', six years after his death; left out as doubtful. The article does not say Ewuare II is his son (the entry does); 'his son' is from the entry.
The article does not say outright in which year he was released from the Lublin prison; the text does not date it.

The entry calls the church Santa Maria di Falleri and places it within the walls; the article describes an 11th-century Benedictine abbey church near the west gate without naming it. The text gives only the article's description.

The saved article is that of the successor body, the National Electoral Institute (INE); only its history up to 2014 and what it says of the IFE are used. The article spells the 1946 body 'Federal Electoral Viligance Commission' (sic); written 'Vigilance' here, which the checker may flag. Present-day INE matters (the 2022 reform proposal, the 2023 Supreme Court ruling, the president's resignation in October 2026) are left out as outside the IFE's years. The redistricting authority is attributed in the article to 'INE' from the early 1990s, i.e. the institute under both names.
The article's list of later accessions gives Salta (4 July 1832) and San Luis (12 July 1832) after Tucumán (18 October 1832), out of date order; the text gives the provinces without dates.

The date of the Jews' move into the Mellah is debated in the article (between the mid-14th and late 16th centuries; many scholars favour the mid-15th, after the 'rediscovery' of Idris II's body in 1437); the text says only 'in the Marinid period', which agrees with the entry's 15th century. The article contradicts itself on the Jewish cemetery (established 1883 at the Mellah's south-west corner; elsewhere moved to the south-east in 1894); left out. Attribution of the New Mechouar (Mohammed ben Abdallah or Moulay Hassan) is disputed; left out. The 1912 Fes riots and the French red-light designation left out for length.
Spellings Dal nAraide / Dál nAraidi and Baetan / Báetáin follow the entry's forms where the article is inconsistent.

The article dates the war 1769-1773 and treats the hostage-taking of 1769 as its first stage; the entry dates it 1772-1773. The text tells the events of 1769-1771 as background and gives no span for the war. The article calls the island's people Kalinago in its lead and its last section but Garifuna in its account of the fighting; the text uses Garifuna, as the entry does. The massacre of an American ship's crew in September 1769 is left out (the article does not say who killed them).

The article's statement that in the 1950s the street was for a time officially considered part of Moore Street (a street on the north side of the city) looks doubtful and is left out. The entry's statement that the street runs through the area of the Viking town is not in the article.

Left out: the section on payments Foraker received from Standard Oil in 1900, which rests on letters published by William Randolph Hearst in 1912 and on one historian's book. The article names the later law the Jones–Shafroth Act; the entry calls it the Jones Act of 1917 (the same law).

The article does not say outright that the fort was named after John Casimir; it notes that Casimir was the name of several Polish kings and of the contemporary John Casimir, and that Stuyvesant encouraged Polish settlers. Worded as 'may honour'.
The article has little on the present site; the last section is brief.

The entry says the couple separated in 1801; the article dates the ultimatum after which they never lived together again to around Christmas 1800. The text gives no year for the separation. The entry says she lived in England until her death; the article says she moved to Paris for a time to live with her son before settling at Exmouth. The Paris stay is left out. The 'Career' heading covers her marriage and household; no other heading on the list fits.

The article names the pope who excommunicated him in 1337 as Benedict XIII, which cannot be right for 1337 (Benedict XII reigned then); the pope is left unnamed. The article gives the fall of Cesena as 21 June without a year, placed next to the fall of Forlì on 4 July 1359; the entry dates Cia degli Ubaldini's defence of Cesena to 1357. No date is given for the fall of Cesena. The article is short (about 280 words); the text uses nearly all of it.

The excerpt gives only the opening of the sections on the governorship; the demarcation under the Treaty of Madrid and the trading company (in the entry) are not repeated. The section 'Return to Lisbon' is empty in the excerpt, so nothing is said of his time as secretary of state.
The article says Seymour insisted the united colony's capital be at New Westminster, and later calls Victoria the united colony's new capital; the capital is not mentioned.

The article gives his birth year as 1853; the entry gives only 'd. 1898', so the birth year is left out. The article's figures for the raid disagree with each other (more than a thousand men, or 22 canoes and 1,500 foot soldiers; 32 white hostages, but more than forty or 43 eaten): only the canoes and Kirk's finding are given.

The article gives his birth year as 1526 and says he died aged 47; the entry gives 1525. Neither the birth year nor the age is printed. The article says Matsura Takanobu expelled him from Hirado in 1558 but also that he baptised over 600 at Hirado between 1558 and 1559; no year is given for either. The article calls Kyoto 'ruled by daimyo Oda Nobunaga' in 1559, which is doubtful; left out.
The article spells the chief of Rams and Dhayah both Hassan bin Ali and Husain bin Ali; he is not named.
The article dates Giulia's marriage to Guidobaldo II both 1535 (lead) and 1534 (body); no year is given.

SKIPPED: article is about the Venetian House of Giustinian as a whole, mostly a list of members, and says almost nothing of the Genoese family association of the Maona of Chios that the entry describes

The article says he must have ascended between 1109 and 1114 CE; the entry dates his reign from c. 1114, so only the 1114 inscription is mentioned. The entry says he issued more land grants than any other ruler of his line; the article does not say this.

SKIPPED: article under 250 words, mostly a debate on the castle's site; it says Tigani shows no trace of a crusader fortress and names Cavo Grosso and Kelefa as candidates, which would contradict the entry's 'probable site at Cape Tigani'

The article says the Māhele allotted one third each to the monarch (crown lands), to the aliʻi and konohiki, and to the makaʻāinana (commoners); the entry says the land was divided among the crown, the government and the chiefs. The shares are not described.

The article's dates for single reigns disagree between its narrative and its list of events (Khidr's overthrow of Nawruz 1360 or 1361; Urus at Sarai 1372 or 1373; Blue Waters 1362 or 1363); those years are left out.
The article says he trained in Argentina in the 1960s but returned to Honduras in 1961; no year is given for his training.

The article is partly written in praise of clan figures (Aidid 'most influential general', 'unlawfully occupied' Somali Region); those judgements were left out. The article lists the Duduble in brackets after the Sifaadle. Living people (Aweys, Ahmed Abdi Karie, K'naan) are named only by their dated roles or not at all. The article does not say that the Hiraab Imamate followed the fall of the Ajuran or name the Abgaal, as the description does; no conflict.

SKIPPED: article is about 300 words and adds little; it disagrees with the entry on when he entered Ottoman service (it says he left Karasi during the interregnum after the 1340s, before the annexation it dates to 1361) and calls the army he routed a Crusader army near the Maritsa, not a Serbian-led one Article: born c. 1305, probably at Balıkesir; died 1365 or 1371; captured Lüleburgaz and possibly Edirne; the battle (Çirmen) dated 1364 by Ottoman chronicles, 1371 by western sources; legend that Lala Şahin Pasha poisoned him. Entry: entered Ottoman service after Karesi's annexation; army 'Serbian-led'.

The article adds that the letter forms could make the inscription as old as the 11th century BCE; left out, as the entry dates him to the 9th century BCE. The article calls him governor, a client king or vassal; the entry says the Akkadian calls him governor and the Aramaic king. Word count about 390.
The article calls the helmet a silver-gilt parade helmet; the entry says a silvered cavalry helmet. Its kind was left unnamed here. Word count about 370.

The article says Umar Tall destroyed the city after taking it in 1862; the entry says it was ruined in the fighting of 1864. The destruction was left undated here. The article is short (about 260 words); the text is just over 260 words.

The article says he 'would have won a majority in his region'; worded here as 'was expected to'. The article does not mention his consideration of acceding to Pakistan or the merger into Rajasthan in 1949 (in the entry). Word count about 360.

The entry says Zambia became a one-party state in 1972; the article gives no year for that and dates the Choma Declaration to 27 June 1973 and the end of the ANC to October 1973. The one-party state is left undated here. Word count about 410.

The article says he was appointed military governor a week before the United States entered the First World War (i.e. March 1917), while the entry has him proclaim the military government in November 1916; the appointment date is left out here. The entry says he commanded US naval forces in European waters during the war; the article dates that command to 4 February 1920, after the armistice, so the command is left out. Word count about 380.

SKIPPED: article has about 230 words of substance, much of it already in the entry Article: Giocangga's residence; Nurhaci built a city there in 1603; khan proclaimed in the Octagonal Hall 1616; capital 1616 to 1622 (the entry implies to 1621); renamed Xingjing 1634; family tombs moved to the Eastern Capital 1624, Giocangga and Taksi brought back 1658; two walls of five and ten li, nine gates; on the Suzi River.

The article's prose summary says Inga inherited the estate Snottsta and that Inga and Eric 'both soon died without leaving any children'; the translation itself says only 'Then she died'. The text follows the translation. Word count about 360.

The article spells the college Banasthali; the entry has Vanasthali. The article also calls him the third prime minister of the United Rajasthan after Manikya Lal Verma; left out as unclear beside 'first chief minister'. Last paragraph is short (about 45 words). Word count about 360.

The article does not give the year of his succession (the entry: 1747). The article does not say outright that Harutoshi succeeded him; it lists him as his son by the concubine Yokoshi. The passage on the elder brother is vague ('killed, because the family crest of another person was similar'); worded cautiously. Word count about 400.

The article is a list of members; it does not mention the governorships of Navarre and Béarn or the dukedom of 1648 (both in the entry). It dates Antoine III's marshalate to 1641. 'Openly bisexual' and 'playboy' left out. A living member (Arnaud, b. 1960) not named. Word count about 320.

The article states that she orchestrated the massacre; the entry attributes it to her faction. The text names the killings without assigning them, and leaves out the massacre's year (the entry: 1879). The article's claim that the British disguised Maung Ba Than as Prince Nyaungok was left out. Word count about 410.
Word count about 370. The article names the successor as Nizamuddin (Nizam-Ud-Din Ahmad III); the entry calls him Nizam Shah; the son is not named here.
The article dates his death 'c. 892' and 'in around 892'; the entry has 892, so no death year is printed here. Word count about 290.

The article contradicts itself on his death: c. 1784 in its opening, 1791–1792 later. No death year is printed. The article's judgement that his motives were 'more commercial than religious' was left out. Word count about 380.
Word count about 400.

The article gives the confiscation as about 12,000 km2 in its lead and as more than 480,000 hectares in its aftermath section; no figure is printed. The excerpt names Cameron without first name or rank, so he is named only as Cameron. The outcome of Ōrākau (the breakout) is not in the excerpt and is not told. Word count about 410.

The entry calls Meskilak his consort; the article agrees and adds that on Failaka his partner may have been Panipa, either the same goddess or a separate one (Krebernik, Glassner). Word count about 380.
SKIPPED: article too thin: under 250 words of substance, a loose founding story of the ruling house, the three religions and a list of residents; nothing to add to the entry

The entry says he sailed from Kosrae. The article says many scholars have concluded he came from Kosrae, but argues this is unlikely (no Kosrae in contact-era navigational lore, no open-ocean sailing, no Kosraean influence on the language), and gives the Marshall Islands or Kiribati as other possibilities. His homeland is left out of the text. The entry spells the thunder god Nahnsapwe; the article has Nansapwe and Nan Sapwe. The text says only 'the thunder god'. Left out: the details of the voyage (Palikir's leftover breadfruit pudding, Likamadau), the suicide's manner, the 1928 Japanese excavation, Petersen's reading that he invaded only Madolenihmw.

The entry dates the Battle of Sulcoit to 967. The article gives 968 in its lead and 967 later (twice: 'the Norse loss in the Battle of Sulcoit in 967', 'dated five years after Sulcoit' for 972). The text leaves Sulcoit undated (it is not mentioned). Left out: the Faelán of uncertain identity, Hudson's and Woolf's readings, Mary Valante's economic reading, the son Aralt and the Battle of Cathair Cuan.
